# The shape of the afternoon

**Two goals, as always:** they leave knowing these tools do far more than they
thought, and believing they can do it themselves on Monday.

- **One afternoon, one paper.** After setup, the cleanup and a short capability
  talk, everything runs on one paper: theirs, or `ai-label-paper` from the course
  files. At Strategy, people sat idle and didn't see the point of the exercises
  (debrief, note 2). On their own paper, every exercise has an obvious point, and
  there is always a next thing to do.
- **The app, not the terminal.** Strategy struggled with the terminal and it
  coloured the rest (debrief, note 1). The Claude app's Code tab is the same agent
  with a window around it; ChatGPT users get Codex in the ChatGPT app.
- **Start a job, talk while it runs, then collect.** *Take it apart* runs while
  you give the sycophancy talk; the three referees run while you give *What it
  can touch*. The talks cost no hands-on time, and nobody waits for an agent
  (debrief, note 3).
- **The referee panel is the centrepiece** (the most engaged block at Strategy),
  now blind, and with sycophancy said out loud (debrief, note 5).
- **Research only.** Francesco: "4 hours methodology only". No teaching block.
  References and DOI checks are in the handout, not the main line (debrief, note 4).
- **No parking lot** (debrief, note 6). Answer at the laptop, or at the very next
  break, the same day.

# Before the day

1. **Room:** A2 Blue 9 (Christine's invitation). Power at every seat; bring
   extension cords.
2. **Reminder email, a week before** (via Christine): *bring a paper in progress,
   as close to submission as you have: a PDF of the draft, plus the Word or LaTeX
   file and the data and code if you can share them. No paper? We have one.*
   And: install the Claude or ChatGPT app beforehand if you can.
3. **Test on a BI-managed Windows laptop:** the list in the README ("To test on a
   Windows laptop"). Above all: does the Claude app install without admin rights,
   and can the agent install git in the user folder?
4. **Pre-run on `ai-label-paper`:** one *Take it apart* and one blind panel, and
   keep the outputs as backups for the projector. The key to what's planted:
   `scratch/examples/ai-label-paper/KEY.md`.
5. **Bring:** sticky notes in two colours (two per person), extension cords, the
   course zip on a USB stick.
6. **Course files:** `course-files.zip` (the handout and the practice folders,
   including `ai-label-paper`). After any change to the handout or a prop:
   re-render, `python3 make-course-files.py`, commit, push.

# Derailments

The rule: **the room's time is for the room.**

- **One-laptop questions** are answered at the laptop.
- **Good questions at the wrong time:** one sentence now, or "at the break", and
  then really at the break. (At Strategy, parked questions were never answered.)
- **Privacy and access:** the privacy slide comes before anyone opens their paper,
  and `access` runs while the referees work.
- **Level differences:** fast people get the next step on their own paper. There
  is always one.

# Module cards

## Get it running

About 25 minutes, first thing.

- **Aim:** by 12:25, every laptop has the app open in a folder, answering, and git
  installed.
- **Floor:** make a file, read it back, delete it, with the folder open in File
  Explorer so they watch it happen.
- **New for Marketing: the app, not the terminal** (Strategy debrief, note 1). It's
  the same agent: the Code tab *is* Claude Code, and the ChatGPT app has Codex. No
  PowerShell, no PATH, no "close and reopen".
- **Not tested on a BI-managed laptop yet:** the README's list. Above all: the
  install without admin rights, and the agent installing git in the user folder.
  The deck and handout are written from Anthropic's desktop docs
  (code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop-quickstart, checked 24 October): the Code tab
  needs Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise; *Local* → **Open folder…**; Ctrl+N for a new
  session; modes *Manual*, *Accept edits*, *Plan*, *Auto*. On native Windows, git
  is optional for the agent itself (it uses PowerShell without it), but we need it
  for save points.
- **Fallback, if the app won't install:** the terminal route at the end of handout
  section 1. The Claude Code install was tested on a BI PC on 14 October: no admin
  rights needed, and the second line puts it on the PATH.
- **Watch for:**
  - a free-plan account (the Code tab asks them to upgrade);
  - Documents synced to OneDrive (use the home folder instead);
  - a session in the wrong folder (the folder control under the prompt box);
  - an old app without the folder control (update it);
  - ChatGPT users: where Codex sits in the ChatGPT app is unchecked. Ask them to
    show you; note it for next time.
- **People with no subscription** pair up. The department reimburses one (receipt
  to Christine); say so.
- **Finished first?** They're the help desk. Or the handout's customer-journey web
  page (untested).

## Do something tedious

About 25 minutes. The prop is `props/decrap-me.zip`, a synthetic WISEflow export:
15 group submissions with junk file names, cover sheets, and an empty grade sheet
in submission order.

- **Aim:** a reorganised folder, a grading table, and one deliberate undo.
- **The framing:** a job the chat window can't do, because it can't touch your
  files. Tedious, local, easy to judge. Kept as the first hands-on task (Strategy
  debrief).
- **Names only.** Group and participant ID are in every folder name, so the job
  needs no reading. In Finance the agent opened the PDFs anyway and the room got
  worked up. The prompts say *"Work from the names only; don't open the
  submissions"*, and the last slide, "You decide what it reads", makes it the
  point.
- **The git beat:** this is their first save point of the day. Brief the task,
  then ask *"Before you hit enter, does anything about this make you nervous?"*
  Answer with *"Set up git here and commit everything."*
- **The undo** is on purpose: delete the Marking guidance folder, then "revert to
  the last commit", with File Explorer open. Watching it come back is what makes
  git stick, and they need the habit for their paper twenty minutes later.

## Your paper

About 15 minutes. The pivot of the afternoon: from here on, everything runs on one
paper.

- **Aim:** everyone has a paper open in a session, described back correctly, with
  a save point.
- **The privacy slide comes first, and fast:** training off, leave out what you
  can't share, tell co-authors. Then move on. The switch labels (*Help improve
  Claude*, *Improve the model for everyone*) weren't verified for December: check
  your own account before the day.
- **Who uses `ai-label-paper`:** anyone without a paper, and anyone whose data they
  can't share. A good hybrid: **their own PDF for the panel, our folder for *Take
  it apart***. Say it out loud; it removes the excuse to sit idle.
- **Watch for:**
  - a Word-only draft: whether the app reads `.docx` without Python is untested.
    If it struggles, *"save it as PDF"*, or let it install a converter;
  - the paper folder inside OneDrive (copy it out);
  - huge data folders (copy only what the paper needs).
- **Done early:** the `AGENTS.md` prompt. It pays off in every later session.

## Take it apart

5 minutes to start, then the sycophancy talk, a break, and 20 minutes to collect.

- **New for Marketing: start it and leave it** (Strategy debrief, note 3). At
  Strategy this was the block that landed, but the room waited for it. The prompt
  writes everything to `take-apart.md`, so the result survives the wait and the
  break.
- **The mode matters:** *Accept edits* or *Auto* before they leave it, or it sits
  waiting for a "yes". Say it twice.
- **On `ai-label-paper`** (the key: `scratch/examples/ai-label-paper/KEY.md`), a
  good run finds:
  - the exclusions beyond the preregistration: with only the preregistered one, the
    candle effect goes from p = .030 to p = .166;
  - the draft's numbers come from an older export (the draft says N = 476; the
    script now gives 545);
  - moderation claimed from simple effects, with no interaction test (p = .346 in
    the draft's own data);
  - the bonus, and the good news: `auth_3` is reverse-worded but not reversed;
    reversed, α goes from .56 to .84.
- **Not yet tested end to end** with this prompt. Pre-run it on `ai-label-paper`
  before the day (Before the day, item 4), and keep the output for the projector.
- **Snags:** the script is R. If R isn't installed, the agent translates it to
  Python or asks to install R; either is fine.
- **The round-up question that matters:** *"Did it find something good for your
  paper?"* It turns the exercise from fault-finding into help.
- **Honest framing:** *"I can't tell you whether a critique of a marketing paper is
  right. You can."* A false alarm is a result too.

## It wants to please you

About 15 minutes, while *Take it apart* runs. A talk, no exercise.

- **The order is the argument:** three forms; why; **the referees are worth having**
  (capability before caveat); status (21%); the companies train against it; our
  measurement; what we learned; what to do. Ends on the panel.
- **Our measurement, said accurately:** two small models (Claude Haiku, GPT-6-Luna),
  one fictional paper with a clear flaw, fresh sessions without profile or memory,
  24 October.
  - Asked for a score under four framings: no difference (means 3.0–3.2 out of 10).
    Pushback, wrongly: 20 of 20 kept the concern.
  - Asked for *feedback* on "my paper, I'm proud of it": the verdict disappears
    (Haiku 10 → 1 of 10, Luna 9 → 0) and praise comes first (0 → 8, 0 → 10). A
    blind judge (GPT-6-Luna, same family as one writer) rated Luna's feedback 1.9
    vs. 4.0 out of 10. All 40 reports still asked for the interaction test.
  - Scripts and aggregates: `scratch/examples/ai-label-paper/sycophancy/`; raw
    reports in `private/sycophancy-runs/`.
- **Don't oversell either way.** Not "they flatter", not "it's solved". The line:
  *asked as a referee, for a verdict, they stayed honest; asked "what do you think
  of my paper?", they coached.*
- **Sources** (checked against the originals, 24 October 2026):
  - Liang et al. (2023), arXiv:2310.01783: overlap 30.85% vs. 28.58% (Nature
    journals), 39.23% vs. 35.25% (ICLR); 57.4% found the feedback helpful; 82.4%
    more beneficial than at least some human reviewers.
  - Vasu et al. (2025), arXiv:2509.13400, Table 2: QwQ-32B, 21.4% of rejects become
    accepts with a stronger affiliation; 7.9% of accepts become rejects with a
    weaker one. Other models differ (DeepSeek R1 8B: 19.05% and 23.02%). 252 ICLR
    2025 papers.
  - OpenAI, GPT-5 System Card (August 2025), section 3.3, Table 4: 0.145 (GPT-4o),
    0.052 (gpt-5-main), 0.040 (gpt-5-thinking); online prevalence −69% (free) and
    −75% (paid) vs. GPT-4o.
  - Sharma et al. (2023), arXiv:2310.13548: the abstract's "both humans and
    preference models prefer convincingly-written sycophantic responses over correct
    ones a non-negligible fraction of the time"; section 3.2, Claude 1.3 wrongly
    admits mistakes on 98% of questions.
  - The GPT-4o rollback dates (rollout 24–25 April 2025, rollback from 28 April) are
    from Codex's reading of OpenAI's two posts (29 April and 2 May); not re-checked
    by hand. Codex's full notes: `private/research/sycophancy-evidence.md`.

## Blind referee panel

20 minutes (package and brief) before the break, 25 (editor and comparison) after.
The centrepiece: at Strategy, the referee panel was the most engaged block of the
two days.

- **Aim:** three reports from fresh sessions in `review-room`, an editor's letter,
  and the comparison with "my paper".
- **Floor:** two reports, and one concern they hadn't thought of.
- **Why a separate folder:** a session reads the project files in its folder and
  the folders above it. `review-room` sits *next to* the paper folder, so the
  referees never see the paper's folder, data or `AGENTS.md`.
- **What else can leak** (tested 24 October, in the terminal, with Haiku in a
  neutral folder): a fresh session sees the user's **profile** in full, the
  **home-folder path** (with the user name), the **account e-mail**, and the list
  of the user's skills. With the profile switched off, the e-mail and the path
  remain. So the paper itself must carry no names (the package step), the brief
  says the paper comes from the editor, and a profile that mentions the paper is a
  leak. The app reads the same settings files; whether it adds more (claude.ai
  preferences, memory) is untested.
- **The check is built in:** the last line of every report answers *"What do you
  know about who wrote or sent this?"* Read a few out in the round-up.
- **Separate sessions, not subagents:** the room can see them, and a main session
  briefing subagents would write their prompts itself ("the user's paper"). What a
  subagent sees wasn't tested.
- **On `ai-label-paper`:** the package step should catch every anonymisation slip
  (KEY item 9), including the PDF's author field and the self-citation. Good
  referees find the missing interaction test, the manipulation check before the
  outcome, and the mediator measured after it.
- **The comparison step** is the sycophancy talk made personal: expect praise first
  and no verdict (our measurement).
- **Skill hook:** "Turn what we just did into a skill called referee-panel". The
  one skill worth making today.

## What it can touch

About 20 minutes, while the three referees run. Talk first; the fence exercise is
optional (handout section 7).

- **The stance, plainly:** lots of access, on purpose. The 50th "yes" is never
  read; git makes mistakes cheap; auto mode stops what matters. Restrict the few
  things that matter, mostly by keeping them out of the folder.
- **In the app:** the mode is a dropdown under the prompt box (*Manual*, *Accept
  edits*, *Plan*, *Auto*; there's also *Bypass permissions*: don't mention it).
  Which mode the Code tab starts in wasn't checked.
- **What we tried** (20 October, terminal versions: Claude Code 2.1.302, Codex
  0.162; the apps run the same agents):
  - Claude, manual: reads in the folder; reading elsewhere, writing, deleting and
    web pages all ask.
  - Claude, auto: edits, Python, reading outside the folder (asks once), a web page,
    `rm -rf data`, even `git reset --hard && git clean -fdx` went ahead. Posting a
    file to an outside address was stopped: *"denied by the Claude Code auto mode
    classifier. Reason: [Data Exfiltration]"*.
  - Codex sandbox (Linux): reads anywhere, writes in the project and `/tmp`,
    network off.
  - The deny rule `Read(./interviews/**)` blocked Claude's Read, `cat`, `cp` and a
    Python one-liner, but `grep -r` printed a transcript. Hence "a fence, not a
    wall".
- **Sources** (official docs, checked 20 October 2026): permission modes and auto
  mode, code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes; settings and rule syntax,
  /permissions and /settings; *"On native Windows, Claude Code runs commands
  unsandboxed"*, /sandboxing; training covers Claude Code, retention 5 years on,
  30 days off, /data-usage; Codex presets and the Windows sandbox,
  learn.chatgpt.com/docs/sandboxing; ChatGPT training controls apply to Codex,
  help.openai.com.
- **Handle with care:** "it sends what it reads" is the honest short version, not
  a guarantee. On personal data, "your consent forms and data plan decide" is safe;
  don't claim what BI's rules say unless you've checked.

# Any time

The handout has all of these (sections 8–17), and each has a deck. Use them for
fast people, for questions, or not at all.

## Git: save points

The full deck (`git`, 25 slides, four exercises) was Strategy's mandatory block.
Today git is one prompt in setup and a habit in the cleanup and the paper; the deck
is for anyone who asks *"how is this different from OneDrive?"*

- **The answer, in one line:** OneDrive is a backup, git is a lab notebook. Keep
  both, but not git inside OneDrive.
- **What a save point is** is the slide people missed in Finance: the files you see
  are always the current version; a commit copies them into `.git`; a revert copies
  a save point back.
- **Sources** (checked 20 October 2026): Torvalds wrote git in April 2005 (*Pro
  Git*, §1.2); Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2022, professional developers: Git
  96.65%; Windows on git, about 300 GB (Brian Harry, Microsoft DevBlogs, May 2017);
  Claude Code checkpoints *"do not track files modified by Bash commands"*
  (code.claude.com, Checkpointing). That last one is why git, not the app's own
  undo, protects the cleanup.

## What it knows about you

- **The profile matters today in one way:** it's read in every session, the
  referees' too. If someone has a profile that names their current paper, they
  switch it off for the panel.
- **The schools question** for marketing (*"grow by targeting a loyal niche, or by
  reaching as many category buyers as possible?"*, Ehrenberg-Bass vs. brand
  equity) is **untested**. Strategy's version changed the framing, not the verdict;
  expect the same.
- **The Berger demo** is the tested example of one line changing the school. Demo
  on Claude: Codex ignored one-line profiles in testing.
- **The deck** (`knows`) still opens with Strategy's "your field, as I imagine it";
  it needs marketing cards before anyone sees it.

- Search: be specific. Deep searches are slow and expensive on usage; show, don't

- DOI check: the practice `.bib` has six traps (key:

  is Bergstrøm & Lind (2023): its DOI belongs to an unrelated 2024 paper.
- Claim check: the centrepiece, on their own draft.
- At Strategy, people were lukewarm about this block (debrief, note 4), so it's

## Leave a trail

About 50 minutes; the key is `scratch/examples/leave-a-trail/README.md`.

- **The practice folder** (`props/messy-project.zip`): three willingness-to-pay
  outliers deleted by hand in Excel, no record. With them, the effect flips sign
  and stops being significant (N = 223, −292 NOK, p = 0.26; without, N = 220, +53
  NOK, p = 0.02). Only the rerun test finds it.
- **Reinhart and Rogoff, accurately:** −0.1% reported above 90% debt to GDP;
  Herndon, Ash and Pollin got +2.2%. The Excel range error accounts for only about
  0.3 points; the rest is excluded years and the weighting. Don't say the Excel
  error alone flipped it.
- **The test** is now a new session, not `/clear`; the same thing in the app.

## Notes and structure

The four questions (from the `tidy-project` skill), the paper folder, `dev/` vs.
`local/`, the log habit. Lighter than the rest.

## Your own work

- **The power-check card** (2 × 2, d = 0.3 vs. 0.1, power for the interaction) is
  the one for this room: it's the `ai-label-paper` problem, in their own design.
  Untested; expect a few hundred per cell, which is the point.
- **Close:** *"What will you try on Monday?"* Three answers out loud.

# Questions you'll get

The longer prepared answers are in `scratch/august-course/grievance-answers.md`.
The short versions:

- **"Is it OK to upload my unpublished paper?"** It's your paper: training off,
  co-authors told, and data you can't share left out. That's the privacy slide in
  *Your paper*.
- **"Can I use this when I referee someone else's paper?"** A different question.
  Many publishers ask referees not to upload manuscripts they review into AI tools.
  Check the journal's policy. Your own paper is yours.
- **"Is my data safe?"** What it reads is sent to the company, like any cloud
  upload. Keep out personal data and confidential material.
- **"Can it read my email?"** Yes, through connectors (MCP): Gmail, Google
  Calendar and Drive connect in a few clicks at `claude.ai/customize/connectors`.
  BI mail is Outlook: a Microsoft 365 connector exists, but BI IT would likely have
  to approve it (not checked). Don't demo on your own work mail.
- **"Does it train on my data?"** It depends on the plan and changes over time, so
  check your plan's terms. When unsure, assume it could be retained.
- **"Claude or ChatGPT?"** Both are excellent. Use the one you pay for. They aren't
  interchangeable, so trying both on the same paper is instructive: they find
  different problems.
- **"Will the department pay?"** Yes: Marketing reimburses a paid Claude or ChatGPT
  subscription. Receipt to Christine.
- **"Can I get the slides?"** Yes: everything is on vibing.jonasmoss.com →
  Marketing, and the handout has every prompt.
